title: Crossing the Bar: occasion
short: Written in October 1889, when Tennyson was eighty, while crossing the Solent; he asked that it end every edition of his poems.
body: Hallam Tennyson's Memoir records that his father wrote the poem in October 1889 on the way from Aldworth to Farringford on the Isle of Wight, after a serious illness; he had 'the moaning of the bar' in mind and showed the poem after dinner, saying it 'came in a moment' (Memoir II, 366, as quoted by Sexton). It was published in Demeter and Other Poems (1889). Shortly before his death in 1892 he told his son to put it at the end of all editions of his poems, and editors have done so since. Musical settings include those by Barnby, Parry and Stanford.

title: one clear call
short: A summons: the call to set out, understood as God's call at death.
body: The 'call' is a summons to depart, as a ship is called to sail; Sexton's notes gloss it as a summons to duty, here that of God. The opening lines name signs of ending (sunset, evening star, call) in short exclamatory phrases without verbs. The evening star (Venus seen after sunset, Hesperus) is the counterpart of the morning star that guides the Dawn in 'Tithonus'; here it signals the close of day.

title: the moaning of the bar
short: A bar is a sandbank at a harbour mouth; waves breaking on it at low tide make a moaning sound.
body: A harbour bar is a ridge of sand or shingle across the mouth of a harbour or estuary, dangerous to cross in rough water or at low tide. Folklore made its moaning an omen of death at sea, as in Charles Kingsley's ballad 'The Three Fishers' (1851), whose refrain returns to the moaning of the harbour bar. Tennyson wishes for no such moaning: no lament, and no struggle in the crossing. The bar is the line between life (the harbour) and the open sea of death and eternity.

title: such a tide as moving seems asleep
short: A full, quiet flood tide that carries a ship easily over the bar, too deep to make noise or foam.
body: At high water the tide is deep enough over the bar for a ship to cross without the turbulence of breaking waves. The paradox 'moving seems asleep' and the phrase 'Too full for sound and foam' make death a gentle passage carried by a force larger than oneself. The tide that comes in from the ocean and then 'Turns again home' is the poem's model of life: it comes from the boundless deep and returns there.

anchor: drew from out the boundless deep
title: the boundless deep ... Turns again home
short: The soul came from the infinite and returns there; compare Wordsworth's 'Ode: Intimations of Immortality'.
body: 'That which drew from out the boundless deep' is the life or soul, imagined as water drawn from the ocean that now returns. The idea that we come from and go back to God recalls Wordsworth's Ode: 'trailing clouds of glory do we come / From God, who is our home'. Tennyson often used 'the deep' for the mystery from which life comes (e.g. 'From the great deep to the great deep he goes' in 'The Coming of Arthur'). 'Turns again home' is set as a short line, giving it the weight of arrival.

title: stanza 3: parallel structure
short: Stanza 3 repeats the pattern of stanza 1, with the evening bell and the dark replacing the star and the call.
body: Each half of the poem opens with a two-stress noun phrase ('Sunset and evening star' / 'Twilight and evening bell'), then an exclamation ('And one clear call' / 'And after that the dark!'), then a wish ('And may there be no...'). The poem alternates long and short lines, and its rhymes run abab. Critics have connected the swelling and shrinking line lengths with the motion of the tide. The 'evening bell' suggests the curfew or a church bell for evening prayer or for a death, deepening the funeral tone, and 'the dark' is the only plain statement of fear in the poem.

anchor: our bourne of Time and Place
title: bourne
short: A boundary or limit; the word recalls Hamlet's 'undiscover'd country from whose bourn / No traveller returns'.
body: 'Bourne' (from French borne, boundary) means a limit or frontier (OED). Here 'our bourne of Time and Place' is the boundary of earthly life, the conditions of space and time that define mortal existence. The word inevitably recalls Hamlet's soliloquy on death, 'The undiscover'd country from whose bourn / No traveller returns' (Hamlet III.i), but Tennyson reverses Hamlet's dread: the flood carries him beyond the boundary, with hope.

title: my Pilot face to face
short: The Pilot is God; to see him 'face to face' echoes St Paul's promise of full knowledge after death.
body: Tennyson explained the Pilot as 'that Divine and Unseen Who is always guiding us' (Memoir II, 366, as quoted by Sexton). The capital letter marks the divine reference. 'Face to face' recalls 1 Corinthians 13:12: 'For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.' The conclusion is a statement of hope rather than certainty ('I hope'), which suits Tennyson's characteristically tentative faith, familiar from In Memoriam.

anchor: When I have crost the bar
title: When I have crost the bar
short: Readers have asked why the pilot appears only after the crossing, since a harbour pilot guides a ship over the bar and then leaves.
body: A harbour pilot normally boards to guide a ship across the bar and disembarks once it reaches open sea, so some readers find the image inverted: the speaker expects to see the Pilot only after crossing. Tennyson's own explanation, as reported, was that the Pilot 'has been on board all the while, but in the dark I have not seen him' (quoted in Hill's Norton edition). On this reading the image is not about navigation at all but about recognition: the guide has been present throughout life and will be seen only beyond it. 'Crost' is an old spelling of 'crossed'.
